rules: General money education only, never personal financial advice. Never recommend a specific stock, coin, fund or product, and never promise returns.
Use simple round example numbers and call them examples. Use only the facts and rules given in the episode idea.
Each episode, Coin teaches Kash one money idea with a tiny everyday story.
Friendly and practical, never preachy. Warn about scams whenever money promises sound too good.
End with one simple action the viewer can take today.

topics: The 50/30/20 budget: about 50% of take-home pay for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings, as a simple starting point.
Emergency fund: many experts suggest saving three to six months of living costs for surprises like a job loss or a broken phone.
Compound interest: your money earns money, and then that money earns money too. The earlier you start, the bigger the snowball (use a simple example).
Pay yourself first: move savings out on payday, before you spend.
Needs versus wants: how to tell the difference before you buy.
Credit cards: if you do not pay the full balance, interest is charged, and it can grow fast.
Inflation: why the same money buys less over time, and why savings left as cash slowly lose value.
The Rule of 72: divide 72 by a yearly growth rate to estimate how many years money takes to double (example: 72 / 8 = 9 years).
How to spot a scam: guaranteed high returns, pressure to act fast, and asking you to keep it secret.
Never share a one-time password (OTP) or PIN, not even with someone claiming to be from your bank.
Diversification: do not put all your eggs in one basket.
Impulse buying: the 24-hour rule, wait one day before buying anything you did not plan.
Track your spending for 30 days: the first step to knowing where your money goes.
Lifestyle creep: when income goes up, spending quietly goes up too.
Teaching kids about money: three jars, one to save, one to spend and one to share.
moreIdeas: Small daily spending adds up: a small amount every day becomes a big amount in a year (simple example).
Good debt versus bad debt: borrowing to build skills or a home can help; borrowing for things that lose value quickly usually hurts.
Index funds explained simply: one fund that holds many companies at once, usually with low fees (education only, not advice).
Sinking funds: save a little each month for big planned costs like school fees, Eid or a new phone.
Earning more: building a skill that people pay for, like design, writing or coding.
Asking for a raise: research the normal pay for your job, show your results, and ask politely.
Insurance basics: paying a small amount to protect yourself from a very big loss.
Opportunity cost: every time you spend money, you give up something else you could have done with it.
Saving for a goal: divide the cost by the number of months to know how much to save each month (example).
Buy now, pay later traps: small instalments can hide fees and lead to overspending.
